text: Chu–Liu / Edmonds: choose, contract, re-weight.

A minimum arborescence (最小树形图) is the cheapest set of directed edges in which every vertex except the root r has exactly one incoming edge and all vertices are reachable from r. Chu–Liu / Edmonds: give each vertex its cheapest incoming edge. If those edges form no cycle, done. Otherwise contract each cycle into one vertex, and for an edge (u, v) entering the cycle at v, reduce its weight by in[v] (choosing it means dropping v's old incoming edge). Repeat. O(nm) (P4716).

If some vertex has no incoming edge at all, there is no arborescence. The weights of the chosen cheapest edges are added to the answer before each contraction; the reduced weights pay the difference later.
A random graph checked against trying every choice of one incoming edge per vertex in Python; the second graph has no edge into vertex 3, so −1.
f[S][v]: merge subsets, relax along edges.

The minimum Steiner tree (最小斯坦纳树): connect k chosen terminal vertices at the lowest total edge weight, using any other vertices as helpers. NP-hard in general, but fine for small k: f[S][v] = cheapest tree that connects the terminal set S and contains v.

Two transitions: merge at v: f[S][v] = min over T ⊂ S of f[T][v] + f[S∖T][v] (O(3k n) over all S); move v along edges: for a fixed S, f[S][·] relaxes like Dijkstra (O(2k m log m)). Answer f[all][any terminal] (P6192).

Checked against trying every subset of the 9 edges in Python. The merge loop over subsets of S is the 3ᵏ part (拓展篇第12章); the Dijkstra part is needed because the cheapest tree may run through non-terminal helpers.
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Arborescence: cheapest in-edge per vertex; no cycle ⇒ done.
2. Cycle: contract; edge into v loses in[v]; repeat; O(nm).
3. A vertex with no in-edge ⇒ impossible.
4. Steiner: f[S][v]; merge f[T][v] + f[S−T][v]; Dijkstra per S.
5. O(3^k n + 2^k m log m).
